decks.title: Matrices — Part 1: Order, types, transpose and symmetry
goals: Write the order of a matrix and locate an entry from its position
Construct a matrix from a rule for its entries
Name the type of a matrix: zero, diagonal, scalar, identity, triangular
Use equality of matrices to find unknowns
Find the transpose and use its laws
Express a square matrix as a symmetric plus a skew-symmetric matrix

slides.heading: Matrices, Part 1
slides.body_md: A rectangular table of numbers, handled as one object.

visual.alt: Table of marks of two imagined students in an Ooty school: Arjun scored 78, 64 and 85 and Bela 55, 90 and 72 in English, Maths and Science.
visual.caption: The same data as the $2 \times 3$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 78 & 64 & 85 \\ 55 & 90 & 72 \end{bmatrix}$.

slides.narration: Welcome to matrices. Look at the marks of two students in three subjects. Written as a rectangular array of numbers, this table becomes a matrix. In this part you will learn how to describe a matrix, the special types of matrices, when two matrices are equal, and a new operation called the transpose.

slides.heading: What you will learn

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: order and entries of a matrix, types of matrices, equality, the transpose, and symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Here is the route. We start with the order of a matrix and how to name each entry, meet the special types, use equality to find unknowns, and finish with the transpose and the symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices that it defines.

slides.heading: Order and position
slides.body_md: A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has **order** $m \times n$. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is written $a_{ij}$.

visual.alt: Grid of positions in a 2 by 3 matrix: row 1 holds a one one, a one two, a one three and row 2 holds a two one, a two two, a two three; the first index is the row and the second the column.
visual.caption: $a_{ij}$ sits in row $i$ and column $j$.

slides.narration: The order of a matrix is written as the number of rows, then the number of columns. Each entry has an address: the first index tells you the row, the second the column. So the entry in row two, column three is called a two three.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a matrix from a rule
slides.body_md: Construct the $3 \times 2$ matrix $A = [a_{ij}]$ with $a_{ij} = 2i + j$.

visual.alt: Table computing a i j equals 2 i plus j for a 3 by 2 matrix: row 1 gives 3 and 4, row 2 gives 5 and 6, row 3 gives 7 and 8.
visual.caption: Fill one cell at a time: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$.

slides.narration: Three rows and two columns means six entries. For each one, put the row number for i and the column number for j into the rule two i plus j. Row one gives three and four, row two gives five and six, and row three gives seven and eight.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a position
slides.body_md: Which number sits in row 3, column 2 of a matrix built from a rule?
slides.narration: Remember: the first index is the row and the second is the column.

slides.heading: Types of matrices
slides.body_md: Row and column matrices, zero matrices, and special square matrices.

visual.alt: Table of types of matrices with a condition and an example for each: row, column, zero, diagonal, scalar, identity, upper triangular and lower triangular matrices.
visual.caption: Every example is checked against its condition by the build.

slides.narration: Some matrices have names. A row matrix has one row and a column matrix has one column. In a zero matrix every entry is zero. Square matrices have more types: diagonal, scalar, identity, and upper or lower triangular. Each name is decided by which entries must be zero or equal.

slides.heading: How the types nest
slides.body_md: Several names can fit one matrix; give the most specific one.

visual.alt: Table of how the special square types nest: an identity matrix is scalar and diagonal; a scalar matrix is diagonal; a diagonal matrix is both upper and lower triangular; a square zero matrix is diagonal, scalar and both triangular.
visual.caption: Choose the most specific name the question asks for.

slides.narration: The square types sit inside each other. Every identity matrix is a scalar matrix, every scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix, and every diagonal matrix is both upper and lower triangular. When a question asks for the type, name the most specific one and give the reason.

slides.heading: Quick check: a scalar matrix
slides.body_md: Which of four 3 by 3 matrices is a scalar matrix?
slides.narration: Look first at the entries off the diagonal, then compare the diagonal entries with each other.

slides.heading: Equality of matrices
slides.body_md: Two matrices are **equal** when they have the same order and every pair of corresponding entries is equal.

visual.alt: Flow for equality of matrices: first check the two matrices have the same order, then equate corresponding entries, solve the equations, and check every entry.
visual.caption: Equal matrices: same order and equal corresponding entries.

slides.narration: Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order and each entry matches the entry in the same position. One matrix equation therefore gives you several ordinary equations, one for each position. That is how we find unknowns.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: unknowns from equality
slides.body_md: Solve $\begin{bmatrix} p + q & 3 \\ s & p - q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 2: entry one one gives p plus q equals 4, entry two two gives p minus q equals 6, so p is 5 and q is minus 1; entry two one gives s equals 2.
visual.caption: Two equations from two entries solve for two unknowns.

slides.narration: Equate the entries one position at a time. The diagonal gives p plus q equals four and p minus q equals six. Adding them, p is five and q is minus one. The bottom left entry gives s equals two. Always check every entry at the end.

slides.heading: The transpose
slides.body_md: The **transpose** $A'$ is obtained by writing the rows of $A$ as columns. If $A$ is $m \times n$, then $A'$ is $n \times m$.

visual.alt: Table showing a 2 by 3 matrix with rows 1, 4, minus 3 and 2, 0, 5, and its transpose, a 3 by 2 matrix whose columns are those rows.
visual.caption: Row $i$ of $A$ becomes column $i$ of $A'$.

slides.narration: To transpose a matrix, write its first row as the first column, its second row as the second column, and so on. A two by three matrix becomes three by two. The entry in position i comma j moves to position j comma i.

slides.heading: Laws of the transpose
slides.body_md: Four laws used again and again.

visual.alt: Table of the four transpose laws: transposing twice gives A back, the transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes, a scalar passes through, and the transpose of a product is the product of transposes in reverse order.
visual.caption: Each law is checked by the build on sample matrices.

slides.narration: Transposing twice gives the original matrix back. The transpose of a sum is the sum of the transposes, and a scalar simply passes through. The important one is the product: the transpose of A times B is B transpose times A transpose, with the order reversed.

slides.heading: Quick check: counting diagonal matrices
slides.body_md: How many 3 by 3 matrices with entries 0 or 1 are diagonal?
slides.narration: Which entries are forced to be zero, and how many choices remain for the rest?

slides.heading: Symmetric and skew-symmetric
slides.body_md: $A$ is **symmetric** if $A' = A$ and **skew-symmetric** if $A' = -A$.

visual.alt: Table of symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices: a symmetric matrix equals its transpose, so it mirrors across the diagonal; a skew-symmetric matrix equals minus its transpose, so mirrored entries change sign and the diagonal is zero.
visual.caption: Look across the leading diagonal.

slides.narration: A square matrix is symmetric when it equals its transpose, so it mirrors across the leading diagonal. It is skew-symmetric when its transpose is its negative: mirrored entries change sign, and every diagonal entry must be zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: splitting a matrix
slides.body_md: Write $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ as $P + Q$, $P$ symmetric and $Q$ skew-symmetric.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 3 with A having rows 5, 3 and minus 1, 4: its transpose, A plus A transpose, the symmetric part P with rows 5, 1 and 1, 4, A minus A transpose, and the skew-symmetric part Q with rows 0, 2 and minus 2, 0.
visual.caption: $P + Q = A$, with $P$ symmetric and $Q$ skew-symmetric.

slides.narration: Every square matrix can be split this way. Find the transpose, then take half of A plus A transpose for the symmetric part, and half of A minus A transpose for the skew-symmetric part. Here P has rows five, one and one, four, and Q has rows zero, two and minus two, zero. Adding them gives A back.

slides.heading: Quick check: the diagonal of a skew-symmetric matrix
slides.body_md: What must every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix be?
slides.narration: Apply the condition to an entry on the diagonal, where the row and column numbers are the same.

slides.heading: Why the split is unique
slides.body_md: If $A = P + Q$ with $P' = P$ and $Q' = -Q$, then $A' = P - Q$, which forces $P = \tfrac12 (A + A')$ and $Q = \tfrac12 (A - A')$.

visual.alt: Flow of the uniqueness argument: if A is P plus Q with P symmetric and Q skew-symmetric, transposing gives A transpose equals P minus Q; adding and subtracting the two equations fixes P and Q, so the split is unique.
visual.caption: Any split must be this one.

slides.narration: Could there be another split? Suppose A equals P plus Q of the right kinds. Transposing gives A transpose equals P minus Q. Adding and subtracting these two equations pins down P and Q exactly, so the split is unique.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Order: rows $\times$ columns; $a_{ij}$ is row $i$, column $j$
Types: zero, diagonal, scalar, identity, triangular
Equal matrices: same order, equal entries

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: order is rows by columns; equal matrices have the same order and equal entries; the transpose turns rows into columns and reverses products; every square matrix splits into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts.
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up. The order is rows by columns, and each entry has a row and column address. Square matrices come in special types. Equal matrices match entry by entry. The transpose turns rows into columns and reverses products. And every square matrix splits into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In equality questions, write **every** equation you use
For a split, show $A'$, $P$ and $Q$, then **check** $P + Q = A$
Name the **most specific** type, with a reason

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: constructing a matrix earns marks for the entries and the matrix; equality earns marks for the equations and values; the split earns marks for the transpose, P, Q and checks; showing symmetry needs the transpose compared.
visual.caption: ISC gives step marks: show each matrix you form.

slides.narration: In the exam, marks follow your working. Write orders the right way round. In equality questions, list each equation you take from the entries. In a split, show the transpose, both parts and the final check. When naming a type, choose the most specific name and give the reason.

decks.title: Matrices — Part 2: Operations and invertible matrices
goals: Multiply compatible matrices of order up to 3
Show that matrix multiplication is not commutative and that non-zero matrices can have a zero product
Decide whether a matrix is singular or non-singular
Verify and find inverses, and prove that an inverse is unique

slides.heading: Matrices, Part 2
slides.body_md: Arithmetic with whole tables of numbers at once.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: adding and scaling matrices, multiplying them, why the order matters, singular and non-singular matrices, and the inverse of a matrix.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Matrices can be added, scaled and multiplied, but multiplication behaves very differently from multiplying numbers. Then we ask when a matrix can be undone: this leads to singular matrices, invertible matrices and a short proof that an inverse is unique.

slides.heading: Addition and scalar multiplication
slides.body_md: $A + B$ adds corresponding entries (same order needed); $kA$ multiplies every entry by $k$.

visual.alt: Table of an imagined Kochi bakery: shop A sold 40, 25, 30 and then 38, 30, 22 of bread, buns and cakes in two weeks, totalling 78, 55, 52; shop B sold 35, 20, 45 and 41, 18, 40, totalling 76, 38, 85.
visual.caption: Adding matrices adds corresponding entries.

slides.narration: Adding two matrices of the same order simply adds the entries in matching positions, like adding two weeks of sales shop by shop. Multiplying by a number scales every entry. These operations behave just like ordinary arithmetic: addition is commutative and associative.

slides.heading: Multiplying matrices
slides.body_md: The $(i, j)$ entry of $AB$ is row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$: multiply in pairs and add.

visual.alt: Table of compatibility: a 2 by 3 times a 3 by 2 gives 2 by 2 while the reverse gives 3 by 3; a 2 by 3 times a 3 by 4 gives 2 by 4 and the reverse is not defined; a 1 by 3 times a 3 by 1 gives 1 by 1 and the reverse 3 by 3.
visual.caption: Inner numbers must match; outer numbers give the order.

slides.narration: To multiply, run along a row of the first matrix and down a column of the second, multiplying pairs and adding. This works only when the number of columns of the first equals the number of rows of the second. The order of the answer comes from the outer numbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a product
slides.body_md: Find $AB$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
bullets: Each entry: one row of $A$ times one column of $B$

visual.alt: Table for worked example 4: each entry of the 2 by 2 product is a row of A times a column of B; the entries are 2, 10, minus 4 and 9.
visual.caption: $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 10 \\ -4 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$, a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

slides.narration: Check the orders first: two by three times three by two gives a two by two answer. Then build each entry. Row one of A with column one of B gives two, and with column two gives ten. Row two gives minus four and nine. Write every entry with its working.

slides.heading: Quick check: a bill as a product
slides.body_md: Find a shopping bill as a row matrix times a column matrix.
slides.narration: Multiply each quantity by its price and add. What order does the answer have?

slides.heading: Order matters
slides.body_md: In general $AB \ne BA$; one of them may not even be defined.

visual.alt: Table for A with rows 1, 3 and 0, 2 and B with rows 2, 0 and 1, 1: A times B has rows 5, 3 and 2, 2, but B times A has rows 2, 6 and 1, 5, so the products differ.
visual.caption: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: $AB \ne BA$.

slides.narration: With numbers, three times five equals five times three. With matrices, the two products usually differ. Here A times B and B times A are both two by two, yet their entries are different. Always keep the order in which matrices are written.

slides.heading: Zero products of non-zero matrices
slides.body_md: $AB = O$ is possible with $A \ne O$ and $B \ne O$.

visual.alt: Table showing two non-zero 2 by 2 matrices, A with rows 3, minus 6 and minus 1, 2 and B with rows 2, 4 and 1, 2, whose product is the zero matrix.
visual.caption: Unlike numbers, $AB = O$ does not force $A = O$ or $B = O$.

slides.narration: Another surprise: two matrices that are not zero can multiply to give the zero matrix. Each row of A meets each column of B in a way that cancels exactly. So you may not conclude that A or B is zero, and you cannot cancel freely in matrix equations.

slides.heading: Quick check: expanding a product
slides.body_md: Expand the product of a sum and a difference of two matrices.
slides.narration: Multiply out term by term, and keep every product in the order it is written.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a matrix equation
slides.body_md: Show that $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 - 9I = O$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 5 with A having rows 1, 4 and 2, minus 1: A squared is 9 times the identity, so A squared minus 9 I is the zero matrix.
visual.caption: So $A^2 - 9I = O$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.

slides.narration: To put a matrix into an expression, replace every number term by that number times the identity. Squaring A gives nine down the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, which is nine times the identity. Subtracting nine I leaves the zero matrix.

slides.heading: Singular and non-singular
slides.body_md: A $2 \times 2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ is **singular** when $ad - bc = 0$ and **non-singular** otherwise.

visual.alt: Table of three 2 by 2 matrices and the number a d minus b c: rows 4, 2 and 6, 3 give 0, so singular; rows 4, 2 and 3, 6 give 18, non-singular; rows 0, 1 and 1, 0 give minus 1, non-singular.
visual.caption: A zero value means singular: one row is a multiple of the other.

slides.narration: For a two by two matrix, the number a d minus b c decides a lot. When it is zero, one row is a multiple of the other and the matrix is called singular. When it is not zero, the matrix is non-singular. The general rule for any order comes in the next chapter.

slides.heading: Invertible matrices
slides.body_md: A square matrix $A$ is **invertible** if there is a matrix $B$ with $AB = BA = I$; then $B = A^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Flow of the definition of an inverse: start with a square matrix A, find B with A times B equal to the identity, check that B times A is also the identity, and then B is the inverse of A.
visual.caption: Both products must give $I$.

slides.narration: A square matrix is invertible when some matrix undoes it from both sides: A times B and B times A are both the identity. That matrix B is the inverse of A. Only square matrices can be invertible, and singular matrices never are.

slides.heading: Quick check: naming the inverse
slides.body_md: What is a matrix B called when A times B and B times A both give the identity?
slides.narration: Recall the definition that both products must satisfy.

slides.heading: The inverse is unique
slides.body_md: If $B$ and $C$ are both inverses of $A$, then $B = C$.

visual.alt: Flow of the proof that an inverse is unique: B equals B times I, which equals B times A C, which by associativity equals B A times C, which is I times C, which is C.
visual.caption: Associativity is the key step.

slides.narration: Suppose B and C are both inverses of A. Start with B, write it as B times I, and replace I by A times C. By associativity this is B A times C, which is I times C, which is C. So a matrix can never have two different inverses.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: an inverse from equations
slides.body_md: Find $A^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ by solving $AB = I$.
bullets: Two equations for each column of $B$

visual.alt: Table for worked example 6: the first column of B solves 3 p plus r equals 1 and 5 p plus 2 r equals 0, giving p equals 2 and r equals minus 5; the second column solves 3 q plus s equals 0 and 5 q plus 2 s equals 1, giving q equals minus 1 and s equals 3.
visual.caption: $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$; check $BA = I$ too.

slides.narration: Write the unknown inverse with four letters and multiply. The first column gives two equations in p and r, the second column two equations in q and s. Solving gives p equals two, r equals minus five, q equals minus one and s equals three. Finally check the product in the other order.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: an inverse from an equation
slides.body_md: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 - 3A + 2I = O$. Find $A^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 7 with A having rows 3, 1 and minus 2, 0: A squared minus 3 A plus 2 I is the zero matrix, so A times 3 I minus A equals 2 I, and the inverse is one half of 3 I minus A, with rows 0, minus 1 and 2, 3 over 2.
visual.caption: A matrix equation can hand you the inverse.

slides.narration: When a matrix satisfies an equation like this one, move the identity term across and factor out A. Here A times three I minus A equals two I. Dividing by two gives the inverse: one half of three I minus A. Multiplying back confirms the answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: summing a product
slides.body_md: Find the sum of the entries of a product of a 2 by 3 and a 3 by 2 matrix.
slides.narration: Find the order of the product first, then compute each entry.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Add or scale entry by entry
$AB$: row times column; columns of $A$ = rows of $B$
$AB \ne BA$ in general; $AB = O$ is possible with non-zero factors
Inverse: $AB = BA = I$, and it is unique

rows: $AB = O$ with $A, B \ne O$ is possible
$AB = BA = I$; unique when it exists

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: a product needs the columns of A to match the rows of B; the order of multiplication matters; two non-zero matrices can multiply to zero; an inverse satisfies A B equals B A equals I and is unique.
visual.caption: Part 2 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up. Addition and scaling work entry by entry. Multiplication goes row by column and needs matching sizes. The order of multiplication matters, and non-zero matrices can multiply to zero. A singular matrix has no inverse, and when an inverse exists it is unique.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State the **order** of a product before computing it
Replace a number term by a multiple of $I$ in matrix equations

rows: each power and multiple, then the result
equations or identity, $A^{-1}$, and the check

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: a product earns marks for each correct entry; showing that the products differ needs both products and a statement; a matrix equation needs each power and multiple; an inverse needs the method, the inverse and a check.
visual.caption: Always verify an inverse by multiplying back.

slides.narration: Some final advice. State the order of a product before you compute it. In matrix equations, a plain number must become that number times the identity. After finding an inverse, multiply back to check. And there is no division of matrices: use associativity and the identity instead.

notes.title: Matrices — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Order, entries and types
sections.body_md:
A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has **order** $m \times n$; $a_{ij}$ is the entry in row $i$, column $j$. A matrix with $mn$ entries can be arranged in as many orders as $mn$ has divisors.

- **Row / column matrix:** one row / one column. **Zero matrix** $O$: every entry $0$.
- **Square** ($m = n$): **diagonal** (off-diagonal entries $0$), **scalar** (diagonal, all diagonal entries equal, $kI$), **identity** $I_n$ (scalar with $k = 1$), **upper / lower triangular** (zero below / above the diagonal).

ISC 2027 uses matrices of order at most $3$.

key_terms.definition_md: A diagonal matrix $kI$ with all diagonal entries equal.

visual.alt: Table of types of matrices with a condition and an example for each: row, column, zero, diagonal, scalar, identity, upper triangular and lower triangular matrices.
visual.caption: Every example is checked against its condition by the build.

visuals.alt: Table of how the special square types nest: an identity matrix is scalar and diagonal; a scalar matrix is diagonal; a diagonal matrix is both upper and lower triangular; a square zero matrix is diagonal, scalar and both triangular.
visuals.caption: Choose the most specific name the question asks for.

sections.heading: 2. Equality and transpose
sections.body_md:
$A = B$ when they have the **same order** and $a_{ij} = b_{ij}$ for every $i, j$: one matrix equation gives several ordinary equations.

The **transpose** $A'$ (order $n \times m$) has $(A')_{ij} = a_{ji}$.

- $(A')' = A$, $\;(A + B)' = A' + B'$, $\;(kA)' = kA'$
- $(AB)' = B'A'$ — the order reverses.

key_terms.definition_md: Rows of $A$ written as columns, written $A'$.

visual.alt: Table of the four transpose laws: transposing twice gives A back, the transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes, a scalar passes through, and the transpose of a product is the product of transposes in reverse order.
visual.caption: Each law is checked by the build on sample matrices.

visuals.alt: Table showing a 2 by 3 matrix with rows 1, 4, minus 3 and 2, 0, 5, and its transpose, a 3 by 2 matrix whose columns are those rows.
visuals.caption: Row $i$ of $A$ becomes column $i$ of $A'$.

sections.heading: 3. Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
sections.body_md:
- **Symmetric:** $A' = A$ ($a_{ij} = a_{ji}$).
- **Skew-symmetric:** $A' = -A$ ($a_{ij} = -a_{ji}$; every diagonal entry is $0$).

For any square $A$: $A + A'$ is symmetric and $A - A'$ is skew-symmetric, since $(A + A')' = A' + A$ and $(A - A')' = -(A - A')$. Hence

$$A = \tfrac12 (A + A') + \tfrac12 (A - A').$$

This split is unique. The only matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric is $O$.

visual.alt: Table of symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices: a symmetric matrix equals its transpose, so it mirrors across the diagonal; a skew-symmetric matrix equals minus its transpose, so mirrored entries change sign and the diagonal is zero.
visual.caption: Look across the leading diagonal.

visuals.alt: Table for worked example 3 with A having rows 5, 3 and minus 1, 4: its transpose, A plus A transpose, the symmetric part P with rows 5, 1 and 1, 4, A minus A transpose, and the skew-symmetric part Q with rows 0, 2 and minus 2, 0.
visuals.caption: $P + Q = A$, with $P$ symmetric and $Q$ skew-symmetric.

sections.heading: 4. Addition, scalar multiplication and multiplication
sections.body_md:
- $A \pm B$ (same order): add or subtract corresponding entries; $A + B = B + A$.
- $kA$: multiply every entry by $k$.
- $AB$ is defined when the number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$; if $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$, then $AB$ is $m \times p$ and $(AB)_{ij}$ = row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$.
- Multiplication is associative and distributes over addition; $AI = IA = A$.
- In a matrix polynomial, a constant $c$ becomes $cI$.

key_terms.definition_md: Columns of the first = rows of the second.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 4: each entry of the 2 by 2 product is a row of A times a column of B; the entries are 2, 10, minus 4 and 9.
visual.caption: $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 10 \\ -4 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$, a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

sections.heading: 6. Singular, non-singular and invertible matrices
sections.body_md:
- A $2 \times 2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ is **singular** if $ad - bc = 0$ (one row a multiple of the other) and **non-singular** otherwise. (The general determinant comes in the next chapter.)
- A square matrix $A$ is **invertible** if $AB = BA = I$ for some $B$; then $B = A^{-1}$. Only square matrices can be invertible; singular matrices are not.
- **Uniqueness:** if $B$ and $C$ are inverses, $B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C$.
- To **verify** an inverse, check both $AB = I$ and $BA = I$. To **find** one: solve $AB = I$ entry by entry, or use a matrix equation such as $A^2 - 3A + 2I = O \Rightarrow A^{-1} = \tfrac12 (3I - A)$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Construct or equate (2 marks):* the entries or equations, then the result.
- *Products (2–3 marks):* each entry carries method; state the order first.
- *Symmetric + skew split (3–5 marks):* $A'$, $P$, $Q$, and the check $P + Q = A$.
- *Inverse (3–5 marks):* the method (equations from $AB = I$ or a matrix equation), $A^{-1}$, and a check by multiplying back.
- *Section D (5 marks):* set in parts such as 2 + 3 or 3 + 2; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing the order as columns $\times$ rows.
- Multiplying corresponding entries instead of rows by columns.
- Assuming $AB = BA$, or expanding $(A + B)^2$ as $A^2 + 2AB + B^2$.
- Writing a constant $c$ instead of $cI$ in a matrix equation.
- Cancelling $A$ from $AB = AC$ when $A$ is not invertible.
- Checking only $AB = I$ when asked to verify an inverse.

questions.stem_md: A librarian in Kohima records how many books each of $4$ classes borrowed on each of the $5$ school days of a week, one row per class. Written as a matrix, the record has order
questions.solution_md: Rows come first: one row for each of the $4$ classes and one column for each of the $5$ days, so the order is $4 \times 5$. The record has $20$ entries, but $20$ is the number of elements, not the order.

questions.stem_md: A matrix has $2$ rows and $3$ columns and every one of its entries is $0$. It is called
questions.solution_md: All entries are $0$, so it is a zero (null) matrix, and its order is rows by columns, $2 \times 3$. Scalar and identity matrices must be square.

questions.stem_md: Four $3 \times 3$ matrices are pinned on a classroom board. Which one is a **scalar** matrix?
questions.solution_md: A scalar matrix is diagonal (every off-diagonal entry $0$) with all diagonal entries equal; here it is $5I_3$. The second is diagonal with unequal diagonal entries, the third has non-zero off-diagonal entries, and the fourth is lower triangular.

questions.stem_md: A $3 \times 2$ matrix $A = [a_{ij}]$ is filled by the rule $a_{ij} = i^2 - j$. Which number sits in row $3$, column $2$?
questions.solution_md: Row $3$, column $2$ means $i = 3$, $j = 2$: $a_{32} = 3^2 - 2 = 7$. The value $1$ comes from swapping the indices ($2^2 - 3$), and that position does not exist in a $3 \times 2$ matrix.

questions.stem_md: Two price lists are equal as matrices: $\begin{bmatrix} 2a - b & 5 \\ 3 & a + b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$. Then
questions.solution_md: Equal matrices have equal corresponding entries: $2a - b = 4$ and $a + b = 5$. Adding, $3a = 9$, so $a = 3$ and $b = 2$.

questions.stem_md: The transpose of the $2 \times 3$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ is
questions.solution_md: The rows become the columns: the first row $1, -2, 4$ becomes the first column, and the second row $0, 3, 5$ the second column, giving a $3 \times 2$ matrix. Refilling the same numbers row by row is not a transpose.

questions.stem_md: A data table $P$ has order $3 \times 4$. A clerk doubles every entry and changes the signs, getting $-2P$, and then transposes it. The order of $(-2P)'$ is
questions.solution_md: Multiplying by a scalar keeps the order $3 \times 4$; transposing swaps rows and columns, so $(-2P)' = -2P'$ has order $4 \times 3$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these matrices is **skew-symmetric**?
questions.solution_md: A skew-symmetric matrix satisfies $A' = -A$: every diagonal entry is $0$ and $a_{ji} = -a_{ij}$. The second matrix is symmetric, the third has a non-zero diagonal entry, and in the fourth $a_{12} = a_{21} = -4$.

questions.stem_md: For which value of $x$ is the seating matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & x + 2 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ symmetric?
questions.solution_md: Symmetric means $a_{12} = a_{21}$: $x + 2 = 5$, so $x = 3$.

questions.stem_md: Every entry on the leading diagonal of a skew-symmetric matrix must be

options.text_md: equal to each other but not necessarily zero

questions.solution_md: $A' = -A$ gives $a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$ for each $i$, so $2a_{ii} = 0$ and $a_{ii} = 0$.

questions.stem_md: A tile pattern is coded by $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 7 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$. Its symmetric part $\tfrac12 (A + A')$ is
questions.solution_md: $A + A' = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$, and half of it is $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$. Forgetting the half gives the second option; the third is the skew-symmetric part $\tfrac12 (A - A')$.

questions.stem_md: For every square matrix $A$, the matrix $A - A'$ is
questions.solution_md: $(A - A')' = A' - (A')' = A' - A = -(A - A')$, which is the definition of skew-symmetric. It is the zero matrix only when $A$ itself is symmetric.

questions.stem_md: In a shop's accounts, $P$ is $2 \times 3$, $Q$ is $3 \times 2$ and $R$ is $2 \times 2$. Which product can **not** be formed?
questions.solution_md: A product $XY$ needs the number of columns of $X$ to equal the number of rows of $Y$. $P$ has $3$ columns but $R$ has $2$ rows, so $PR$ is not defined; $PQ$ ($2 \times 2$), $QR$ ($3 \times 2$) and $RP$ ($2 \times 3$) are.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, then the product $AB$ is
questions.solution_md: Row by column: row 1 of $A$ with the columns of $B$ gives $4 - 1 = 3$ and $0 - 2 = -2$; row 2 gives $8 + 3 = 11$ and $0 + 6 = 6$. The second option is $BA$, and the third multiplies matching entries, which is not matrix multiplication.

questions.stem_md: At a ration shop in Madurai, Rani buys $2$ kg of rice, $3$ kg of dal and $1$ litre of oil at ₹$50$, ₹$120$ and ₹$160$ per unit. Her bill is the product of the row matrix of quantities and the column matrix of prices, which is
questions.solution_md: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 50 \\ 120 \\ 160 \end{bmatrix} = [\,2(50) + 3(120) + 1(160)\,] = [\,620\,]$, a $1 \times 1$ matrix: the bill is ₹$620$.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -6 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, which statement is correct?

questions.stem_md: A shear of a grid is described by $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Applying it three times corresponds to $A^3 =$
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^3 = A^2 A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: each multiplication adds $1$ to the top-right entry. Cubing each entry would give $A$ again, which is wrong.

questions.stem_md: For square matrices $X$ and $Y$ of the same order, the product $(X + Y)(X - Y)$ always equals
questions.solution_md: Expanding term by term and keeping the order of each product: $(X + Y)(X - Y) = X^2 - XY + YX - Y^2$. It reduces to $X^2 - Y^2$ only when $XY = YX$.

questions.stem_md: The matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 - 5A + kI = O$. The value of $k$ is
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $5A = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$, so $A^2 - 5A = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 \end{bmatrix} = -7I$. Hence $k = 7$.

questions.stem_md: A $2 \times 2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ is singular when $ad - bc = 0$. Which of these is **singular**?
questions.solution_md: $6(2) - 4(3) = 0$, so the first matrix is singular (its second row is half its first). The others give $10$, $-1$ and $1$, all non-zero.

questions.stem_md: Which matrix $B$ satisfies $AB = BA = I$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$?
questions.solution_md: Check the product: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 - 5 & -10 + 10 \\ 3 - 3 & -5 + 6 \end{bmatrix} = I$, and the product in the other order is $I$ too. The third option gives $-I$.

questions.stem_md: Square matrices $A$ and $B$ of order $3$ satisfy $AB = BA = I_3$. Then $B$ is called
questions.solution_md: This is the definition: $B$ is the inverse of $A$, written $A^{-1}$, and $A$ is then invertible (non-singular).

questions.stem_md: $A$ is an invertible square matrix and $B$, $C$ are matrices of the same order with $AB = AC$. What follows?

options.text_md: nothing can be concluded about $B$ and $C$

questions.solution_md: Multiply $AB = AC$ on the left by $A^{-1}$: $A^{-1}AB = A^{-1}AC$, so $IB = IC$ and $B = C$. Cancellation is allowed precisely because $A^{-1}$ exists.

questions.solution_md: Singular means $ad - bc = 0$: $3\lambda - 12 = 0$, so $\lambda = 4$.

questions.solution_md: Skew-symmetric needs $a_{12} = -a_{21}$, so $a = -3$.

questions.solution_md: Each diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix is $0$, so their sum is $0$.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, the entry in row $2$, column $1$ of $A^2$ is ____.
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: row 2 of $A$ times column 1 of $A$ is $2(1) + 1(2) = 4$.

questions.stem_md: Every entry of a $3 \times 3$ matrix is $0$ or $1$. How many such matrices are **diagonal** (all off-diagonal entries $0$)?
questions.solution_md: The six off-diagonal entries must be $0$; each of the three diagonal entries can be $0$ or $1$: $2^3 = 8$ (the zero matrix and $I_3$ included).

questions.solution_md: The order $m \times n$ needs $mn = 18$: $1 \times 18$, $18 \times 1$, $2 \times 9$, $9 \times 2$, $3 \times 6$, $6 \times 3$, so there are $6$ orders.

questions.solution_md: $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 7 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, so the sum of its entries is $2 + 7 - 1 + 2 = 10$.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, the matrix $AA'$ is symmetric. What is its entry in row $2$, column $2$?
questions.solution_md: Row 2 of $A$ times column 2 of $A'$ (which is row 2 of $A$ again): $3^2 + 1^2 = 10$. In full, $AA' = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ 5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.solution_md: The diagonal must be $0$, and the three entries above the diagonal decide the three below (with opposite signs). Each of $a_{12}, a_{13}, a_{23}$ has $3$ choices: $3^3 = 27$.

questions.stem_md: Find the positive value of $\lambda$ for which $\begin{bmatrix} \lambda & 3 \\ 4 & \lambda + 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is singular.
questions.solution_md: $\lambda(\lambda + 1) - 12 = 0$, i.e. $\lambda^2 + \lambda - 12 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 4) = 0$. So $\lambda = 3$ or $\lambda = -4$; the positive value is $3$.

questions.stem_md: A weather station stores the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$. Express $A$ as the sum of a symmetric matrix $P$ and a skew-symmetric matrix $Q$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$A' = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$.

$P = \tfrac12 (A + A') = \tfrac12 \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 6 \\ 6 & -4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, which is symmetric.

$Q = \tfrac12 (A - A') = \tfrac12 \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, which is skew-symmetric.

Check: $P + Q = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = A$.

$(A - A')' = A' - (A')' = A' - A = -(A - A')$, so $A - A'$ is skew-symmetric.

If $B' = B$ and $B' = -B$, then $B = -B$, so $2B = O$ and $B = O$.

questions.stem_md: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. By writing $B = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix}$ and solving $AB = I$, find $A^{-1}$, and check that $BA = I$.

A $3 \times 3$ matrix used by a traffic study in Nagpur is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

(a) Find $A'$, $P = \tfrac12 (A + A')$ and $Q = \tfrac12 (A - A')$. [3]

(b) Show that $P$ is symmetric, $Q$ is skew-symmetric and $P + Q = A$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $A' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 & -4 \\ -6 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

$A + A' = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & -4 \\ 4 & 6 & -2 \\ -4 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, so $P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

$A - A' = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 & -8 \\ -4 & 0 & 6 \\ 8 & -6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, so $Q = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & -4 \\ -2 & 0 & 3 \\ 4 & -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

**(b)** $P' = P$ (entries mirror across the diagonal), and $Q' = -Q$ (zero diagonal, mirrored entries change sign).

$P + Q = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = A$.

(b) Hence show that $A$ is invertible and find $A^{-1}$. Verify your answer. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ -5 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$ and $5A = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 5 \\ -5 & 15 \end{bmatrix}$, so $A^2 - 5A = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 \end{bmatrix} = -7I$, i.e. $A^2 - 5A + 7I = O$.

**(b)** Rearranging, $A(5I - A) = 7I = (5I - A)A$. So $A \cdot \tfrac17 (5I - A) = I = \tfrac17 (5I - A) \cdot A$, which shows $A$ is invertible with

$A^{-1} = \tfrac17 (5I - A) = \frac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

Check: $A \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = 7I$.
